title: Adab with creation
hookLine: a cat shut in and left hungry, a dog at a well, and a leather sock full of water

cards: A cat, shut in. No food set down, and no way out to hunt for its own.
That's the whole story, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, in paraphrase: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said a woman entered the Fire because of a cat.
She neither fed it nor let it loose to eat the small creatures of the earth. No crime against a person. No grand sin anyone would whisper about.
One animal, in her power, and ignored.

teach.b: Start with the Qur'an's view of animals. Surah al-An'am, in Pickthall's translation: "There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you."
Peoples: communities with their own lives, not furniture in ours. Now put the cat beside a second story, also in Bukhari, in paraphrase. A man walking along a road grew desperately thirsty.
He found a well, climbed down, and drank. Climbing out, he saw a dog panting, licking damp earth from thirst. He thought: this dog is suffering what I just suffered.

So he went back down, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth to climb, and gave the dog a drink. And the Prophet said Allah thanked him for it, and forgave him. The companions were surprised.
They asked: is there reward for us even in animals?
His answer, in paraphrase: in every living thing with a moist liver, there is reward. A body that is alive; that's the whole qualification.
The two stories mirror each other. One person had an animal in her control and did nothing. One had no duty to a stray dog at all, and went back down the well.
Adab with creation lives in the space between: when something weaker is thirsty in front of you, noticing it, the way the man noticed: this is what I just felt.

how: Islamic teaching on animals draws on Qur'an 6:38, which calls animals and birds peoples like us, and on hadith such as the woman and the cat and the man who gave water to a thirsty dog.

o: the story of how Allah created the heavens and the earth
the care owed to every living thing, not only to people
the rules for which animals may be eaten and which may not

games.q: adab with creation — tap the pairs.
p: given water in a leather sock

s: the woman's sin was a crime against another person
it was a cat she shut in and neither fed nor let loose to find food.
the man saw in the dog the thirst he had just felt
he thought: this dog is suffering what I just suffered, and went back down the well.
the companions assumed animals counted for reward
they were surprised and asked: is there reward for us even in animals?

games.q: you've just climbed out of a well after a desperate drink. a dog is panting beside it, licking damp earth. you have no bucket. what do you do?
o: go back down and carry water up in your leather sock.
call someone else to deal with it.
games.why: he filled his sock, held it in his teeth to climb, and gave the dog a drink. Allah thanked him and forgave him.

practice: Bring to mind the animals that cross your day: a pet asleep on the couch, pigeons at the bus stop, a stray cat under a parked car.
Choose one and ask the man's question at the well: what does this creature need that I happen to have, water in a bowl, crumbs where it's allowed, a fresh dish set down with attention?
If you pray, you can remember that creature in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Adab with creation. The manners owed to every living thing: not leaving it hungry in your power, and going back down the well when it's thirsty. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a moist liver, the hadith's phrase for any living thing.

carryVoice: Your line: every creature counts. Anything with a moist liver is in the circle. Tomorrow, adab with the earth.
